query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys containing at least five elements (each ≥5 at.%), the magnitude of local lattice distortion—arising from differences in atomic radii—controls the superconducting transition temperature by modulating the electron-phonon coupling strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A known Nb-Ta based superconducting high-entropy alloy (e.g., a refractory HEA with a random solid solution structure) exhibiting moderate lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloys with constant overall valence electron count (VEC) but with systematically varied atomic size mismatch (and hence lattice distortion) through adjustments in composition.
generation.conditions: Solid solution maintained; minimum of five elements present at no less than 5 atomic percent each; single-phase structure; ambient pressure and temperature conditions applicable to conventional superconductivity measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion quantified by atomic size variance and its effects on the lattice (e.g., measured by diffraction techniques and EXAFS).
generation.mechanism: Larger atomic size differences induce greater local lattice distortion, which in turn disrupts the characteristic lattice vibrations (phonon modes). This disruption reduces the electron-phonon coupling efficiency that is critical for Cooper pair formation, leading to a lower superconducting transition temperature (Tc).
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with increased atomic size mismatch (and hence higher lattice distortion) will exhibit a lower Tc compared to baseline alloys with lower mismatch when other factors such as VEC are held constant.
generation.baseline: A well-studied Nb-Ta based superconducting HEA that demonstrates a moderate level of lattice distortion and a known Tc.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where the HEA remains a homogeneous single-phase solid solution; it may not extend to systems with partial ordering or where additional mechanisms (such as strong electron correlations) dominate superconducting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between lattice distortion magnitude and Tc is not fully established. Additionally, other factors such as detailed phonon spectra or minor secondary phases might also influence Tc.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloys with identical VEC and similar processing conditions but varying levels of atomic size mismatch (controlled via compositional adjustments). Characterize the local lattice distortion using X-ray/neutron diffraction and pair distribution function or EXAFS measurements, and determine the superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) using resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements.
measurements: Quantitative atomic size variance / local lattice distortion metrics (from diffraction or EXAFS analysis)
Superconducting Tc (via resistivity and magnetic susceptibility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variation in Tc is not observed with increasing measured lattice distortion—for instance, if alloys with higher lattice distortion display similar or even higher Tc compared to lower-distortion alloys—then the hypothesis that lattice distortion is the dominant factor controlling superconductivity would be falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.
